items.title: 9.2 Sum and Difference Formulas for Inverse Trigonometric Functions

source_refs.note: Book p. 269-272: 9.2 Sum and Difference Formulas, formulas (i)-(vi) with proofs, Remember! box, Examples 8-11

blocks.text: In this section, we will derive the addition and subtraction formulas for inverse trigonometric functions. These identities can be derived by applying the fundamental trigonometric identities along with algebraic manipulation. These identities are valid only within the principal value of the respective inverse trigonometric functions. We will now establish the sum and difference formulas for the inverse sine, cosine and tangent functions that are given below.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Start from the basics: \(\sin^{-1}x\) is an angle, the angle in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) whose sine is \(x\). So \(\sin^{-1}x + \sin^{-1}y\) is simply the sum of two angles.
We already know the sine, cosine and tangent of a sum of two angles (the Remember! box). Every proof in this section uses the same three moves:
1. Give each inverse a name, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), and write \(\sin\alpha = x\), \(\sin\beta = y\) (or cos, or tan).
2. Apply the ordinary trigonometric formula to \(\alpha + \beta\) or \(\alpha - \beta\).
3. Take the inverse function of both sides to come back to inverse functions.
Why do we need these formulas? They join two inverse functions into one. That is how identities with numbers are proved (Exercise 9.2) and how equations such as Example 11 are solved.

blocks.text_alt: (i) inverse sine of x plus inverse sine of y equals inverse sine of (x times root of 1 minus y squared, plus y times root of 1 minus x squared)
(ii) inverse sine of x minus inverse sine of y equals inverse sine of (x times root of 1 minus y squared, minus y times root of 1 minus x squared)
(iii) inverse cosine of x plus inverse cosine of y equals inverse cosine of (x y minus root of (1 minus x squared) times (1 minus y squared))
(iv) inverse cosine of x minus inverse cosine of y equals inverse cosine of (x y plus root of (1 minus x squared) times (1 minus y squared))
(v) inverse tangent of x plus inverse tangent of y equals inverse tangent of (x plus y) over (1 minus x y)
(vi) inverse tangent of x minus inverse tangent of y equals inverse tangent of (x minus y) over (1 plus x y)

blocks.title: Remember!
blocks.text:
\(\sin(\alpha \pm \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta) \pm \cos\alpha\sin\beta\)
\(\cos(\alpha \pm \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta \pm \sin\alpha\sin\beta\)
\(\tan(\alpha \pm \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha \pm \tan\beta}{1 \pm \tan\alpha\tan\beta}\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The Remember! box has three slips.
1. A stray bracket in the sine formula. Correct: \(\sin(\alpha \pm \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta \pm \cos\alpha\sin\beta\).
2. The sign in the cosine formula must be the opposite one: \(\cos(\alpha \pm \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta \mp \sin\alpha\sin\beta\). Test with \(\alpha = \beta = \frac{\pi}{4}\): \(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0\), and \(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 0\), but \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1\).
3. The sign in the tangent denominator must also be the opposite one: \(\tan(\alpha \pm \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha \pm \tan\beta}{1 \mp \tan\alpha\tan\beta}\). The proof of formula (v) below uses the correct form \(1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
When does each formula hold? The book says the identities are valid only within the principal values but does not give the conditions. The right side of each formula is always a principal value (for \(\sin^{-1}\) it lies in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\)), so the left side must land in the same interval. The table below lists the conditions (we checked them numerically for many thousands of values).
Example: \(\tan^{-1}2 + \tan^{-1}3 \approx 1.1071 + 1.2490 = 2.3562\), which is \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\). Formula (v) would give \(\tan^{-1}\frac{5}{-5} = \tan^{-1}(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{4}\): wrong, because \(xy = 6 > 1\).
In Questions 1 to 9 of Exercise 9.2 every pair of numbers satisfies its condition.

blocks.caption: Conditions for the formulas (our addition, not printed in the book); in (i) to (iv) also \(-1 \le x, y \le 1\)

blocks.text: To prove (i), we proceed as follow:

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 'we proceed as follow'. Correct English: 'we proceed as follows'.

Let
\[\sin^{-1}x = \alpha \Rightarrow \sin\alpha = x\]
and
\[\sin^{-1}y = \beta \Rightarrow \sin\beta = y\]

Now
\[\cos\alpha = \pm\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}\alpha}\]
\[= \pm\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\]
Since \(\alpha, \beta \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), so \(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta \ge 0\)
\[\therefore\ \cos\alpha = \sqrt{1-x^{2}}\]
Similarly, \(\cos\beta = \sqrt{1-y^{2}}\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why can the \(\pm\) be dropped? \(\alpha = \sin^{-1}x\) is a principal value, so \(-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \alpha \le \frac{\pi}{2}\): the angle is in the first or fourth quadrant, where cosine is never negative. This is the step where principal values enter every proof. For \(\cos^{-1}\) the angle is in \([0, \pi]\), so there it is the sine that is never negative.

Now
\[\sin(\alpha+\beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\]
\[\sin(\alpha+\beta) = x\sqrt{1-y^{2}} + y\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\]
\[\Rightarrow \alpha + \beta\]
\[= \sin^{-1}\left(x\sqrt{1-y^{2}} + y\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)\]
Thus,
\[\sin^{-1}x + \sin^{-1}y\]
\[= \sin^{-1}\left(x\sqrt{1-y^{2}} + y\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The step \(\sin(\alpha + \beta) = k \Rightarrow \alpha + \beta = \sin^{-1}k\) is allowed only when \(\alpha + \beta\) itself lies in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\). For positive \(x\) and \(y\) this is exactly the condition \(x^{2} + y^{2} \le 1\) in the table. For instance \(\sin^{-1}1 + \sin^{-1}1 = \pi\), but the formula gives \(\sin^{-1}0 = 0\).
Similarly, we can prove (ii), (iii) and (iv).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How the other three go (try them yourself first):
(ii) Same start as (i), but use \(\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta\).
(iii) Let \(\cos^{-1}x = \alpha\), \(\cos^{-1}y = \beta\). Now \(\alpha, \beta \in [0, \pi]\), so \(\sin\alpha = \sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) and \(\sin\beta = \sqrt{1-y^{2}}\) (sine is not negative there). Then \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta = xy - \sqrt{(1-x^{2})(1-y^{2})}\); take \(\cos^{-1}\).
(iv) The same, with \(\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\).

Next, we proceed to prove formula (v) as follows:
Let
\[\tan^{-1}x = \alpha \Rightarrow \tan\alpha = x\]
and
\[\tan^{-1}y = \beta \Rightarrow \tan\beta = y\]
Now
\[\tan(\alpha+\beta) = \dfrac{\tan\alpha + \tan\beta}{1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta}\]
\[\tan(\alpha+\beta) = \dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}\]
\[\Rightarrow \alpha+\beta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}\]
Thus,
\[\tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y\]
\[= \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Formula (v) needs \(1 - xy \ne 0\), otherwise the fraction is undefined, and in fact \(xy < 1\) (see the table). If \(x, y > 0\) and \(xy > 1\), the true value is \(\pi + \tan^{-1}\frac{x+y}{1-xy}\).

Further by putting \(y = x\) in (v), we get
\[\tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}x\]
\[= \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x+x}{1-xx}\]
\[\Rightarrow 2\tan^{-1}x = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1-x^{2}}\]
Similarly, we can prove (vi).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: For (vi) take the same \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) and use \(\tan(\alpha - \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha - \tan\beta}{1 + \tan\alpha\tan\beta} = \frac{x - y}{1 + xy}\). For the double result \(2\tan^{-1}x = \tan^{-1}\frac{2x}{1-x^{2}}\), the condition \(xy < 1\) with \(y = x\) becomes \(x^{2} < 1\), that is \(-1 < x < 1\). We use this result in Exercise 9.2 Questions 6 and 8.

In a similar way, the following results can be derived from (i) and (ii)
\[2\sin^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\left(2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)\]
and
\[2\cos^{-1}x = \cos^{-1}\left(2x^{2}-1\right)\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says both results come 'from (i) and (ii)'. Only the first comes from (i). Putting \(y = x\) in (ii) gives just \(\sin^{-1}0 = 0\). The second result comes from (iii): with \(y = x\), \(x \cdot x - \sqrt{(1-x^{2})(1-x^{2})} = x^{2} - (1 - x^{2}) = 2x^{2} - 1\). So it should read 'from (i) and (iii)'.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Deriving the first result: put \(y = x\) in (i): \(x\sqrt{1-x^{2}} + x\sqrt{1-x^{2}} = 2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\).
Conditions (not printed): \(2\sin^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}(2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}})\) needs \(|x| \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so that \(2\alpha\) stays in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\). \(2\cos^{-1}x = \cos^{-1}(2x^{2}-1)\) needs \(0 \le x \le 1\), so that \(2\alpha\) stays in \([0, \pi]\).
Test: \(x = 1\) in the first gives \(2\sin^{-1}1 = \pi\) on the left but \(\sin^{-1}0 = 0\) on the right.

blocks.title: Example 8
steps:
Given: the angle \(\cos^{-1}x\), where \(-1 \le x \le 1\).
To prove: \(\cos^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\).
Method: give the angle a name, \(\alpha = \cos^{-1}x\). Find \(\sin\alpha\) from \(\sin^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\alpha = 1\), then take \(\sin^{-1}\) of both sides. This is how a \(\cos^{-1}\) is changed into a \(\sin^{-1}\).

Name the angle
\[\alpha = \cos^{-1}x\]
\[\cos\alpha = x\]
Why: \(y = \cos^{-1}x\) if and only if \(x = \cos y\), with \(y\) in \([0, \pi]\). So \(\alpha\) lies in \([0, \pi]\).

Find \(\sin\alpha\)
\[\sin\alpha = \sqrt{1-\cos^{2}\alpha}\]
\[= \sqrt{1-x^{2}}\]
Why: \(\sin^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\alpha = 1\). We take the positive root because \(\alpha \in [0, \pi]\), and sine is never negative there.

Take \(\sin^{-1}\) of both sides
\[\Rightarrow \alpha = \sin^{-1}\left(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)\]
\[\therefore\ \cos^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\left(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)\]
Why: \(\sin\alpha = k\) gives \(\alpha = \sin^{-1}k\) only when \(\alpha\) is in the principal range \([-\pi/2, \pi/2]\). Together with \(\alpha \in [0, \pi]\) this needs \(0 \le \alpha \le \pi/2\), that is \(0 \le x \le 1\). The book does not state this condition (see the Book correction below).

Check with \(x = \frac{1}{2}\)
\[\cos^{-1}\tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{\pi}{3}\]
\[\sin^{-1}\sqrt{1-\tfrac{1}{4}} = \sin^{-1}\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]
\[= \tfrac{\pi}{3}\ \checkmark\]
Why: both sides give the same angle, \(60^{\circ}\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book states \(\cos^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) with no condition, as if it held for every \(x\) in \([-1, 1]\). It holds only for \(0 \le x \le 1\). For \(-1 \le x < 0\) the angle \(\cos^{-1}x\) is more than \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), but \(\sin^{-1}\) never gives more than \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Example: \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{2\pi}{3}\), while \(\sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}\). Correct statement: \(\cos^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\), and \(\cos^{-1}x = \pi - \sin^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) for \(-1 \le x < 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The same triangle idea turns any inverse function into another. If \(\alpha = \cos^{-1}x\) with \(0 < x < 1\), draw a right triangle with adjacent side \(x\) and hypotenuse 1. The opposite side is \(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\), so \(\alpha = \sin^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}} = \tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\). This is exactly what Exercise 9.2 needs when the answer is in a different inverse function from the question.

blocks.title: Example 9
steps:
Given: the angles \(\sin^{-1}\frac{5}{13}\) and \(\sin^{-1}\frac{12}{13}\).
To prove: their sum is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).
Method: both terms are \(\sin^{-1}\) of a number, added, so formula (i) fits: \(\sin^{-1}x + \sin^{-1}y = \sin^{-1}\left(x\sqrt{1-y^{2}} + y\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)\). Its condition holds: \(x^{2} + y^{2} = \frac{25}{169} + \frac{144}{169} = 1 \le 1\).

Name the numbers
\[x = \tfrac{5}{13},\quad y = \tfrac{12}{13}\]
Why: with names, substituting into formula (i) is mechanical.

Work out the two square roots
\[\sqrt{1-y^{2}} = \sqrt{1-\tfrac{144}{169}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{25}{169}}\]
\[= \tfrac{5}{13}\]
\[\sqrt{1-x^{2}} = \sqrt{1-\tfrac{25}{169}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{144}{169}}\]
\[= \tfrac{12}{13}\]
Why: these are the roots inside formula (i). The book squares \(\frac{12}{13}\) and \(\frac{5}{13}\) inside the bracket; doing it first keeps each line short. (5, 12, 13 is a Pythagorean triple: \(5^{2} + 12^{2} = 13^{2}\).)

Substitute into formula (i)
\[\sin^{-1}\tfrac{5}{13} + \sin^{-1}\tfrac{12}{13}\]
\[= \sin^{-1}\left(\tfrac{5}{13}\cdot\tfrac{5}{13} + \tfrac{12}{13}\cdot\tfrac{12}{13}\right)\]
\[= \sin^{-1}\left(\tfrac{25}{169} + \tfrac{144}{169}\right)\]
\[= \sin^{-1}\left(\tfrac{169}{169}\right) = \sin^{-1}(1)\]
\[= \tfrac{\pi}{2}\]
Why: \(x\sqrt{1-y^{2}} = \frac{5}{13}\cdot\frac{5}{13}\) and \(y\sqrt{1-x^{2}} = \frac{12}{13}\cdot\frac{12}{13}\). Finally \(\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) is in the principal range \([-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}]\).

Check
\[\sin^{-1}\tfrac{5}{13} \approx 0.3948\]
\[\sin^{-1}\tfrac{12}{13} \approx 1.1760\]
\[0.3948 + 1.1760 = 1.5708 \approx \tfrac{\pi}{2}\ \checkmark\]
Why: a calculator in radian mode agrees. Another way: in the 5, 12, 13 triangle, \(\sin^{-1}\frac{12}{13} = \cos^{-1}\frac{5}{13}\), and \(\sin^{-1}u + \cos^{-1}u = \frac{\pi}{2}\) (Example 5).

blocks.title: Example 10
steps:
Given: the expression \(\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{y} - \tan^{-1}\frac{x-y}{x+y}\).
To prove: it equals \(\frac{\pi}{4}\).
Method: a difference of two \(\tan^{-1}\) terms, so use formula (vi): \(\tan^{-1}a - \tan^{-1}b = \tan^{-1}\frac{a-b}{1+ab}\) with \(a = \frac{x}{y}\), \(b = \frac{x-y}{x+y}\). Then simplify the compound fraction using the common denominator \(y(x+y)\).

Apply formula (vi)
\[\text{L.H.S} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{\dfrac{x}{y} - \dfrac{x-y}{x+y}}{1 + \dfrac{x}{y}\cdot\dfrac{x-y}{x+y}}\]
Why: \(a - b\) goes on top and \(1 + ab\) at the bottom. We call the numbers \(a\) and \(b\) here so they are not confused with the \(x\) and \(y\) of the question.

Simplify the top
\[\tfrac{x}{y} - \tfrac{x-y}{x+y} = \dfrac{x(x+y) - y(x-y)}{y(x+y)}\]
\[= \dfrac{x^{2} + xy - yx + y^{2}}{y(x+y)}\]
Why: the common denominator of \(y\) and \(x+y\) is \(y(x+y)\). Note \(-y(x-y) = -yx + y^{2}\).

Simplify the bottom (as printed)
\[1 + \tfrac{x}{y}\cdot\tfrac{x-y}{x+y}\]
\[= \dfrac{yx + y^{2} + x^{2} + xy}{y(x+y)}\]
Why: \(1 = \frac{y(x+y)}{y(x+y)} = \frac{yx + y^{2}}{y(x+y)}\) and \(\frac{x}{y}\cdot\frac{x-y}{x+y} = \frac{x^{2} - xy}{y(x+y)}\). So the last term must be \(-xy\); the book prints \(+xy\) (see the Book correction below). Correctly, the bottom is \(\frac{x^{2} + y^{2}}{y(x+y)}\).

Cancel the common denominator (as printed)
\[= \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x^{2} + xy - xy + y^{2}}{xy + y^{2} + x^{2} + xy}\right)\]
\[= \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x^{2} + y^{2}}{x^{2} + y^{2}}\right)\]
Why: top and bottom share the denominator \(y(x+y)\), so it cancels. On top \(xy - xy = 0\); at the bottom the correct \(xy - xy = 0\) also cancels, which is why the next line is \(\frac{x^{2} + y^{2}}{x^{2} + y^{2}}\).

Finish
\[= \tan^{-1}(1) = \tfrac{\pi}{4} = \text{R.H.S}\]
Why: \(\tan\frac{\pi}{4} = 1\) and \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) is in the principal range \((-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2})\).

Check with \(x = 3,\ y = 1\)
\[\tan^{-1}3 - \tan^{-1}\tfrac{2}{4}\]
\[\approx 1.2490 - 0.4636 = 0.7854\]
\[\tfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.7854\ \checkmark\]
Why: with numbers in place of letters the identity can be tested on a calculator (radian mode).
book_errors: \[= \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x^{2} + xy - xy + y^{2}}{xy + y^{2} + x^{2} + xy}\right)\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the working the book prints the denominator \(yx + y^{2} + x^{2} + xy\) and on the next line \(xy + y^{2} + x^{2} + xy\). Both should end in \(-xy\): \(y(x+y) + x(x-y) = xy + y^{2} + x^{2} - xy = x^{2} + y^{2}\). The book's next line \(\tan^{-1}\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\) and the result \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) are correct. The book also gives no condition: formula (vi) needs \(ab > -1\), which here means \(y(x+y) > 0\) (true, for example, when \(x, y > 0\)). For \(x = 1,\ y = -\frac{1}{2}\) the left side equals \(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\), not \(\frac{\pi}{4}\).

blocks.title: Example 11
steps:
Given: \(\tan^{-1}\frac{x-1}{x+1} + \tan^{-1}\frac{2x}{x+1} = \frac{\pi}{4}\), with \(x \ne -1\).
To find: every \(x\) that satisfies the equation.
Method: join the two angles into one with formula (v), take \(\tan\) of both sides, and solve the algebraic equation that results. Formula (v) only holds when \(ab < 1\), so every root must be tested in the original equation.

Join the two terms with formula (v)
\[\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\dfrac{x-1}{x+1} + \dfrac{2x}{x+1}}{1 - \dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\cdot\dfrac{2x}{x+1}} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\]
Why: \(\tan^{-1}a + \tan^{-1}b = \tan^{-1}\frac{a+b}{1-ab}\) with \(a = \frac{x-1}{x+1}\), \(b = \frac{2x}{x+1}\).

Simplify the top
\[\dfrac{x-1}{x+1} + \dfrac{2x}{x+1} = \dfrac{3x-1}{x+1}\]
Why: the denominators are the same, so add the numerators: \((x - 1) + 2x = 3x - 1\).

Take tan of both sides
\[\dfrac{3x-1}{x+1}\cdot\dfrac{(x+1)^{2}}{-x^{2}+4x+1} = \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\]
\[\Rightarrow \dfrac{3x-1}{x+1}\cdot\dfrac{(x+1)^{2}}{-x^{2}+4x+1} = 1\]
Why: if \(\tan^{-1}u = \frac{\pi}{4}\) then \(u = \tan\frac{\pi}{4} = 1\). Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.

Clear the fractions
\[(3x-1)(x+1) = -x^{2} + 4x + 1\]
\[3x^{2} + 2x - 1 = -x^{2} + 4x + 1\]
\[4x^{2} - 2x - 2 = 0\]
\[2x^{2} - x - 1 = 0\]
Why: cancel one factor \((x+1)\) (allowed, \(x \ne -1\)), cross-multiply, bring every term to the left, then divide by 2.

Factorise
\[(x-1)(2x+1) = 0\]
\[x - 1 = 0 \text{ or } 2x + 1 = 0\]
\[x = 1 \text{ or } x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\]
Why: split the middle term, \(2x^{2} - 2x + x - 1 = 2x(x-1) + 1(x-1)\).

Test \(x = -\frac{1}{2}\) in the original equation
\[\tfrac{x-1}{x+1} = \tfrac{-3/2}{1/2} = -3\]
\[\tfrac{2x}{x+1} = \tfrac{-1}{1/2} = -2\]
\[\tan^{-1}(-3) + \tan^{-1}(-2) = -\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\]
Why: both angles are negative, so their sum cannot be \(+\frac{\pi}{4}\). Here \(ab = (-3)(-2) = 6 > 1\), so formula (v) did not hold; that is how this false root entered. So \(x = -\frac{1}{2}\) does not satisfy the equation.

Check \(x = 1\)
\[\tan^{-1}\tfrac{0}{2} + \tan^{-1}\tfrac{2}{2} = 0 + \tfrac{\pi}{4}\]
\[= \tfrac{\pi}{4}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(x = 1\) satisfies the original equation. Thus \(x = 1\) is the only solution.
blocks.answer: \(x = 1\) is the only solution (\(x = -\frac{1}{2}\) does not satisfy the equation).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: In an equation with inverse functions always substitute every root back into the original equation and write one line for each: 'satisfies' or 'does not satisfy'. Examiners give a mark for rejecting the false root with a reason.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Six formulas: (i), (ii) for \(\sin^{-1}x \pm \sin^{-1}y\); (iii), (iv) for \(\cos^{-1}x \pm \cos^{-1}y\); (v), (vi) for \(\tan^{-1}x \pm \tan^{-1}y\).
2. Method of proof: name the angles \(\alpha, \beta\); use the sum or difference formula of sin, cos or tan; take the inverse function of both sides.
3. The positive square root is taken because of the principal ranges: cosine is not negative on \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), sine is not negative on \([0, \pi]\).
4. Each formula has a condition; the most used: (v) needs \(xy < 1\), (vi) needs \(xy > -1\).
5. Double results: \(2\tan^{-1}x = \tan^{-1}\frac{2x}{1-x^{2}}\) (\(|x| < 1\)), \(2\sin^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}(2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}})\), \(2\cos^{-1}x = \cos^{-1}(2x^{2}-1)\).
6. \(\cos^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\) (Example 8).
7. In equations, test every root in the original equation (Example 11).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\sin^{-1}x + \sin^{-1}y = \sin^{-1}(x + y)\). Inverse functions do not add like that; use formula (i).
2. Writing \(2\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{4} = \tan^{-1}\frac{2}{4}\). The 2 doubles the angle, not the number: use \(\tan^{-1}\frac{2x}{1-x^{2}}\).
3. Using \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\) (as in the misprinted Remember! box). For a sum the sign is minus.
4. Using formula (v) when \(xy > 1\): \(\tan^{-1}2 + \tan^{-1}3\) is \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\), not \(-\frac{\pi}{4}\).
5. Keeping a root such as \(x = -\frac{1}{2}\) in Example 11 without testing it.
